strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 9 benchmarks with consistent methodology and multiple model scales (4B-14B), providing robust evidence of improvements
Significant practical efficiency gains (4-4.3× speedup, 70.8%-83.7% token reduction) demonstrated even with vLLM-accelerated baselines, validating the core advantage
Training-free approach with elegant closed-form solution for input-output alignment (W_a) via ridge regression, enabling immediate application to pre-trained models
Well-designed ablations demonstrating necessity of alignment (+2.3%-5.3% gains) and analysis of optimal latent step depth; effective case study illustrating error propagation in multi-agent pipelines
Clear presentation with thorough documentation, including detailed prompts, implementation details, and prompt templates for reproducibility
Practical solution to a genuine bottleneck in multi-agent LLM systems, with clear complexity analysis (Theorem 3.4) showing orders-of-magnitude theoretical efficiency gains
weaknesses: Theoretical contributions rely on restrictive, unvalidated assumptions: Theorem 3.1 depends on Linear Representation Hypothesis with ternary coefficients not empirically confirmed; Theorem 3.3 is a straightforward application of known KV-cache properties with limited novelty; Theorem 3.4's comparison assumes exact expressiveness equivalence unnecessary for good performance

Strict requirement for homogeneous agents (identical architecture across all models) severely limits real-world applicability; proposed adapter solution undermines 'training-free' claim and remains unvalidated experimentally

Mixed and modest empirical improvements, especially on complex reasoning tasks: minimal gains on AIME25 (0-3.3%), GPQA-Diamond (0.5-3.9%); improvements concentrated on simpler tasks (ARC-E +2.2%), suggesting efficiency gain rather than reasoning improvement

The claim of 'lossless information preservation' is incomplete and potentially misleading: only guaranteed at KV-cache level; latent-to-embedding conversion via W_a introduces transformation; no analysis of error accumulation through agent chains

Limited baseline comparisons—only text-based MAS and single models; missing comparisons with other latent communication schemes, hybrid approaches, or other efficient MAS frameworks; unclear whether 'training-free' advantage holds against all alternatives

Semantic consistency validation (Figure 5) relies on 2D t-SNE projections without quantitative metrics; case study (Appendix D) suggests TextMAS failure may stem from prompt design rather than fundamental text communication limitation

No code release mentioned; hyperparameter selection (λ, latent step depth) lacks justification or sensitivity analysis; generalization only demonstrated on Qwen3 family; no analysis of when LatentMAS should or should not be applied

strengths: Novel framework for latent collaboration in multi-agent LLM systems with clear motivation and strong practical benefits (4×-4.3× speedup, 70.8-83.7% token reduction, +13.3-14.6% accuracy)
Comprehensive theoretical analysis with formal expressiveness bounds (Theorem 3.1), information preservation guarantees (Theorem 3.3), and complexity analysis (Theorem 3.4)
Extensive empirical evaluation across 9 diverse benchmarks (math, science, reasoning, code), multiple model scales (4B-14B), and MAS architectures, with proper baselines and multiple runs
Thorough ablation studies including input-output alignment analysis (Figure 6), semantic meaning verification (Figure 5), optimal latent step depth analysis, and qualitative case studies
Training-free method with practical applicability to existing models using standard HuggingFace interfaces; detailed implementation details and prompts provided for reproducibility
Consistent empirical gains across diverse tasks and model scales, with speedup maintained even when baselines are optimized with vLLM acceleration
weaknesses: Significant unexplained gap between theoretical predictions (235×-471× efficiency for Qwen models from Theorem 3.1) and empirical speedup (4×-4.3×), suggesting theory doesn't capture practical bottlenecks or assumptions are overly optimistic

Restrictive homogeneous agent requirement (identical architecture and hidden dimensions) limits practical applicability; heterogeneous support only briefly mentioned in appendix as future work requiring trainable adapters

Limited novelty in individual components: Theorem 3.3 on information preservation is essentially definitional (KV caches by design preserve recomputed representations), and the W_a alignment is a relatively standard ridge regression formulation

Insufficient analysis of actual information preservation: claims of 'lossless transfer' are unverified empirically; no probing tasks or measurements of degradation when latent representations diverge from intended semantics

Missing experimental comparisons with related methods: KVComm (Fu et al., 2025) and other recent latent communication approaches are cited but not compared, making it difficult to assess relative merit
Linear Representation Hypothesis (Assumption B.1) with ternary coefficients is restrictive and not validated empirically; unclear if real hidden representations actually follow this structure

Limited analysis of failure cases: many tasks show only marginal improvements (1-3%), some show no improvement or degradation; insufficient discussion of task characteristics determining when latent vs. text collaboration helps
Reproducibility concerns: no mention of code release, ridge regression hyperparameter λ requires tuning with limited guidance, and some implementation details remain vague
